transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: We wanna just kinda knock on. Alright. Rodriguez just dropped out.

transcript.name: Announcer
transcript.text: Five candidates remain in a fractured democrat field, just days from the primary to decide who will take on likely republican nominee Tom Tiffany. Tonight, their first and only televised debate at a critical juncture in Wisconsin history. Former lieutenant governor Mandela Barnes.

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: We've been all across Wisconsin taking the fight directly to Tom Tiffany.

transcript.name: Announcer
transcript.text: Former Tony Evers cabinet member, Joel Brennan.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: And I am in this race, and I'm committed to continuing in this race because Wisconsin values are at risk.

transcript.name: Announcer
transcript.text: Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley. Wisconsin,

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: you deserve a true Democratic candidate, and that's exactly why I am reentering this race.

transcript.name: Announcer
transcript.text: State representative Francesca Hong.

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: I am the only candidate in this race who takes income and power inequality seriously as the most urgent crisis of our times.

transcript.name: Announcer
transcript.text: State Senator Kelda Roys.

transcript.name: Kelda Roys
transcript.text: That was not the time to move backwards and be in more disarray.

transcript.name: Announcer
transcript.text: And now, live from the campus of Marquette University in Milwaukee. Tonight's moderators, WISN twelve political director Matt Smith and up front cohost twelve news anchor Gerron Jordan.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Thank our audience across Wisconsin for joining us for the first and only televised debate between the Democratic candidates in the primary for Wisconsin governor. Mandela Barnes, Joel Brennan, David Crowley, Francesca Hong and Kelda Roys. We thank you all for being here with us tonight.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: The top vote getter in the August primary will take on the likely Republican nominee Tom Tiffany in November, with Tony Evers not seeking reelection. It is the first wide open race for governor since 2010. First tonight, a few ground rules. This is a debate, but we'll be having a conversation. We'll be discussing some of the key issues facing Wisconsin.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Candidates are asked to state their positions, stay on topic and to be concise. The candidates may speak to each other, but we will manage the time on any given topic and move the conversation along if necessary.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: At the end, each candidate will make a brief closing statement. It is fair to say that this race has been chaotic over the last few weeks, so let's get right to it.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Mr Crowley, three weeks ago you dropped out of this race saying you couldn't see a path to victory. Eleven days ago, the primary upended when Sara Rodriguez dropped out and you made the unprecedented move of reentering the race with an immediate endorsement from Governor Tony Evers. Since then, you have been linked to a social media account that includes offensive posts. You've said you didn't write any of those, and some have accused you of being the latest prop for the Democratic establishment. So are you and why should voters now trust your judgment and ability to win?

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: Well, first and foremost, thank you for having us, but I was never born into the establishment. I was actually born into struggle. I grew up in the 53206 zip code where I had to work extremely hard for everything that I have, and so I'm not here to protect the establishment. I'm here to deliver real results for Wisconsinites all over our states. And, you know, I like to make decisions based off of the data, based off of facts.

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: And we learned ever since that day that a lot of things have changed, and we were going off of false data. And so we know that the stakes are too high this upcoming election, and that's why I got back into this race. And I'm honored to not only have the endorsement of governor Tony Evers, but lay labor unions and leaders all across this state who believe in my leadership, and I'm looking forward to delivering for all of Wisconsin.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Miss Hong, you are the Democratic Socialist who is leading in all the polls, yet some Democrats are attempting to stop you from winning, fearful that you cannot beat Republican Tom Tiffany. Just this weekend, the co chair of the Democratic Socialists of America, which you are a member, reaffirmed the DSA's position of abolishing the senate, prisons, and replacing the presidency and the supreme court as we know it. Do you fully back the DSA platform, and why should primary voters trust your judgment and your ability to win statewide?

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: Well, first, thank you so much to the team at WISN, the Marquette University for hosting this important debate. I do not support the full platform of the National DSA, and I'm not endorsed by DSA National. What democratic socialism is is a form of government that puts working class people first, that puts work first. The policies that we have been working on, permanent affordability, has broad bipartisan support in every corner of the state. Well, things like fully funding our public schools, ensuring that we are doing right by our kids and cutting property taxes.

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: Taxing the ultra wealthy and mega corporations, ensuring that we can invest in free childcare, and that everyone has access to affordable housing. And we are the only campaign to support a moratorium on AI data centers, and we have found broad bipartisan support. I am looking forward to helping the Democrats become the big tent party that they've aimed to be for many years.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Mr Barnes, you were once seen as the clear front runner in this race. You previously lost a statewide election for US Senate when the field cleared for you. In fact, last year, the Milwaukee Courier said we need a candidate who can unite this state and win. Mandela Barnes already showed us he can't, and Governor Tony Evers recently endorsed David Crowley over you. So why should primary voters now trust you that you can win statewide this time?

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: Well, thanks so much for the question and thanks so much for having me. There's not a single person on this stage who's united all shades of blue of the Democratic Party as I have before. Now that race in 2022, it was the closest US Senate race in the state in over one hundred years. It was the closest challenge to any incumbent across the entire country. No incumbent lost statewide.

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: Now while DC insiders like Chuck Schumer didn't see the race as winnable, Republican billionaires certainly did. They spent over $50,000,000 to defeat me, and I only lost by one point, 26,000 votes. Now I can tell you, having been the only person on this stage who's actually won statewide in 2018 when we kicked Scott Walker out of office for good, that race was also decided by one point. Now I've been on both sides of the coin, and you learn a whole lot more when you lose. When you win, you think you did everything right.

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: But when you come up that short, you have a whole lot of time to think about the things that went wrong. You learn about the devastating impact of big money in politics. You also learn about how low Republicans can get, and I can tell you right now we have the resources and we have the support to get it done and on the terms of governor Evers, I have zero interest in upholding the status quo. I have zero interest in being the establishment candidate. That is the difference right here on the stage because I am pushing the envelope to make sure that we are as bold as we can possibly be in the Donald Trump era because that's what people have been calling for Democrats to be all along.

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: We have not truly met the moment.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Mister Brennan and miss Roys, you are both polling in the single digits and have been since the start of this race. At this point, are primary voters wasting their vote on a vote for you, mister Brennan?

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: Well, here's what I would tell you is I don't think primary voters have been paying much attention until the last two weeks and all the upheaval that you have seen. This is what I find when I am going out around the state is that, and this has been verified by polls that was done here by my alma mater at Marquette, because about half the people at this point haven't made a decision. And so that is a lane that's opening up. The challenge that I have had from day one is not that anybody thinks I'm unqualified for the office. I am I served as the top appointee to Governor Evers.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: We created the largest budget surplus in state history. We increased the rainy day fund. We got millions billions of dollars out to family farms, to small businesses, to renters who needed it during COVID. So all of that stuff puts me in good stead. The challenge I have had is that people don't know me as well as they know some other candidates around the state.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: And so what I have found in recent days is that the disruption, the upheaval, somebody putting their thumb on the scale, it has gotten people much more engaged and much more interested in this race. And day by day I am feeling that momentum and I'm feeling people who want somebody who can beat Tom Tiffany in the fall and who can hit the ground running on day one. And I I will put my qualifications on those issues up against anybody in this race.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Mister Brennan, thank you. Miss Roys, you are continuing to poll in the single digits as well. At this point, are primary voters wasting their vote on a vote for you?

transcript.name: Kelda Roys
transcript.text: If you want the best public schools in the nation for your children, if you want to open up the state's health care plan so that everyone can buy in and we can lower costs for all Wisconsinites, if you want a candidate who is gonna stand up and fight Donald Trump and bring an end to this authoritarian regime, then you should vote for me. I am the candidate in this race that brings the most experience in and around state government with ten years of service in the legislature and the only one who served on the state budget committee. I've also been an executive in the private and nonprofit sectors, and for over twenty years, I've been the candidate that has turned progressive ideas, like the kind that all of us have on this stage, into law. That kind of experience is absolutely essential, and voters need to think about not just who can beat Tom Tiffany, although that is important, Not just who can deliver a democratic legislature, although that is vitally important, but who can actually do the job on day one. And I am proud to have earned by far the most endorsements of any candidate in this race, including the most endorsements in Milwaukee County, the most, largest labor union endorsement with WEAC, the state teachers union, and, the endorsement of former lieutenant governor Barbara Lawton.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Thank you all. Last week, a Madison police officer shot and killed a man. Tonight, the investigation and the protests continue. Governor Tony Evers has called for transparency and accountability and urged for peaceful protests. Miss Hong in the hours following the shooting, standing alongside protesters, you said quote this state sanctioned violence was an execution.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Would you make those immediate declarations as governor even though an investigation had not yet started?

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: No, the governor has the largest microphone in the state and there comes deep responsibility with that. But what we saw in videos and what I had talked to folks who had witnessed that, I think what we saw, it was clearly the type of violence where no one's life should have been taken. My thoughts are with, Corey Ruys and his family, and I hope that the accountability and transparency that both the governor Evers and I have called for, the independent investigation, the investment in body cameras. We want local governments to be able to invest in public safety, to be serious about public safety, and I plan to be a partner in that.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: You have also called to defund and abolish police before while saying your ideal world is one without prisons. Would you sign a bill or budget that cuts funding for police departments? No. No, why not?

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: The governor cannot defund police, and I'm not here to govern by slogan. I'm here to make sure that I am the governor that is most serious about public safety, That means investing in the things that we know prevent crime and getting resources to victims and ensuring that the people who are incarcerated and the folks who are working in our prisons are able to live a life of dignity and work with dignity. I think it's important that we invest in communities, including our public schools, out of of school programs, and mental health resources, and attacking the opioid, epidemic. These these are things that are proven to prevent crime, and this is what will help to make sure that we have a government that is serious about public safety.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Mister Barnes, you have previously shown support for reducing police funding and abolishing ICE. Following the Madison shooting, you said you were deeply disturbed and pained. Would you sign a bill or budget that cuts funding for police departments?

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: First of all, we should all be very disturbed by what we saw in those images, what we saw in the video. And we should fight as hard as we possibly can as a state, as a people, as a society, to make sure that never happens again. And body cameras, of course, are the norm. It should be the norm. And I wish that the Madison Police Department did have those body cameras.

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: So of course, I would not sign a budget that reduced funding because obviously that police department needs the funding to have body cameras.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Miss Roys, after the Madison shooting, you said we do not have to accept this as inevitable. We can create a more fair, safe world. Would you sign a bill or budget that cuts funding for police departments?

transcript.name: Kelda Roys
transcript.text: No, but I think we need to actually fund local communities so that we can do evidence based programs that actually reduce and prevent crime. At the end of the day, I'm a mom and stepmom of five. I want my kids and every kid to be safe in our communities, and I want law enforcement officers to be safe in our communities. That means that we have to invest in proven strategies that actually do that, unlike what Republicans like Tom Tiffany have done, which is cut funding to local governments, and take away local control so that communities don't have the resources to be able to actually solve these problems effectively. I am really proud, as the only attorney on this stage, to be someone that has fought for and passed criminal justice reforms to make us more safe and more just.

transcript.name: Kelda Roys
transcript.text: I have taken on racial disparities in areas from health to criminal justice, and I believe that Wisconsin can be a place where everyone has the freedom to thrive, but not if we aren't willing to tackle these really tough issues.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Mr. Brennan, after the shooting in Madison, you are also calling for investigation. Would you sign a bill or a budget that cuts funding for police departments?

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: Of course I wouldn't. And I think as others have said here, there's been a generation of disinvestment and a broken system between the state, the broken partnership between state and local government. So we need to make sure that we're robustly funding that. It has been demonstrated. This hundred and fifteen year old contract that we have had between state and local government worked pretty well for the first eighty years.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: And then the Republicans just turned off the spigot and stopped funding local government. So we need to make sure we do that. On the larger issue of criminal justice reform, we need to look a little bit to our neighbors to the West. In Minnesota, they spend about $215 per capita on criminal justice in that state. They they're about the same size.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: They have about the same crime rate. We have about three times as many people incarcerated. In Wisconsin, we spend about $315 per capita on that. As a long term target, spending that $600,000,000 difference that they spend on other things in Minnesota, spending those on early childhood, on K-twelve education, on other programs in Wisconsin, that would be the kind of investment over the long term that would put us in better stead and keep us from having fewer of these incidents. Because they should outrage all of us, but there are ways that we can make a difference on those by spending our money differently.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Brennan, thank you. Mr. Crowley, without first seeing any video, you said that you were horrified by the reports of the shooting and immediately pointed to other police shootings in Kenosha and Minneapolis. Did you rush to judgment with your comments, and would you sign a bill or budget that cuts funding for police departments?

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: No. Did not rush to judgment with my comments. My thoughts and prayers are not just with Corey and his family and friends, but with the entire Madison community and everybody who's been affected and retraumatized by this. Again, we have seen these types of incidents happening here locally with Jacob Blake, as well as George Floyd in Minnesota. And so it's extremely important that we have transparency.

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: We cannot defund the police. We should be investing in public safety, and that doesn't mean more money to police officers. That's like investing in in in in in systems like the community violence interruption. Milwaukee County, we have been a leader in actually helping to reduce violent crime here in Milwaukee County, working directly hand in hand with not just police departments, but also community organizations. And so we have to focus on not just investing upstream, but making sure we wrap around services around families so that they don't have to go down the road of criminality in the first place.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Madison Police currently do not have police body cameras. Raise your hand if, as governor, you would sign legislation requiring all police and sheriff's departments in Wisconsin to have body cameras.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: All of you

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: all candidates.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Let's move on to the economy tonight. Wisconsinites overwhelmingly say inflation and the cost of living is the most important issue ahead of this election. The failed tax relief deal negotiated by Governor Tony Evers and Republican leaders who have delivered rebate checks to Wisconsinites, directed money to local schools to lower property taxes, increased special education funding, and eliminated taxes on tips and overtime. It failed in the state Senate. I'd like you to raise your hand if as governor you would have signed that deal into law if it passed.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: If it passed, if it passed, would you have signed it into law? One, Mr. Crowley.

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: Miss Roys, you were one of the 15 Democratic senators who helped kill the deal. Why?

transcript.name: Kelda Roys
transcript.text: Because at the end of the day, my job is to be a responsible steward of taxpayer dollars, and this would have created a $2,900,000,000 deficit down the road, which our schools and our health care system and our local governments cannot afford. It also would have spent the surplus before it even materialized. Look at what is happening with the economy. When we are spending money that we do not yet have and spending it in ways that do not actually help us solve the long term problem of getting more money into our public schools, giving property tax relief to property taxpayers, and making sure that we have a more fair, just tax system, All we are doing is throwing that money away on a political gimmick that was frankly cooked up by Robin Vos as he sees the blue wave coming and wanted to do anything that he could to either protect his members from losing their seats and run away from their terrible record on public education, which Tom Tiffany is partially responsible for.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Quickly, that projected deficit factored in zero economic growth. Would you consider zero economic growth? Would that be part of a Roys administration if you cite that deficit?

transcript.name: Kelda Roys
transcript.text: I'm looking at having a president who is hell bent on making things as expensive and challenging for families across the state, and a congressman running for governor who has done nothing but rubber stamp Trump's agenda 100%.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Thank you. Mr. Crowley, you're the only one who raised your hand to sign the deal. Why would you have signed it into law?

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: Well, would have signed it into law because we would have gotten a bipartisan deal actually done. I think folks understand here in the state of Wisconsin when you have divided government, it can be a bit chaotic. Were there things in this bill that I did not like? Absolutely. I love the fact that we were going to give relief into our schools and property tax relief, and there are other things in this bill that I didn't like.

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: At the end of the day, we know that there are many Wisconsin families who are desperate. We should be focusing on how we lift them up and not playing politics. And so I would have signed that bill because that means it would have passed with bipartisanship.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Congressman Tom Tiffany is campaigning on the fact that he would return the entire surplus, he says, to taxpayers. Miss Hong, would you return the surplus to taxpayers, or how would you spend the projected $2,500,000,000

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: Those are the taxpayers dollars, but investment is what we need, thinking about our shared future, our kids. It is an investment when we invest in public schools and ensuring that we are cutting property taxes, but doing right for our kids. Our campaign is about permanent affordability, and putting all of those surplus dollars, back into, taxpayers money. I think that it would be irresponsible, and the reason why that surplus deal was so problematic is that those who are on fixed income would not have received that check. Folks who are lower income would have received less.

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: I think it's important to think about some of the working class families across our state that deserve real relief, durable relief, and that deal was not it.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: We should mention you did vote against that in the assembly. Quickly, what would you spend the surplus on?

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: Public education and health care.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Mister Brennan, would you return it to the taxpayers, or would you spend it, and how would you spend it?

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: Well, I think Tom Tiffany, and the Republicans have already shown their hands about how they'd return it to the taxpayers. There are three sections in the studio audience here tonight. If the poor people were and the people on fixed income and Social Security were sitting over here, they would get nothing. The rest of us who are doing okay would get the $306,100 dollars. And by the way, if you want a stimulating effect by putting money into the economy, you put it in the hands of people who are going to spend it.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: And so that was part of the deal. The thing that I would have exercised in all of this is caution. Because we live in a Trump economy. I put together as a secretary of administration two budgets for governor Evers, and we need to make sure that we are doing everything possible to be cautious in this time with Trump. The way that I would spend it, you know, one, it would be cautious.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: But the first thing that I would spend, the first $100,000,000, which I will do in January, will go into child care and early childhood education. It is a system that is broken. A billion dollars of productivity sits on the sidelines every year from especially from women, mainly from women who can't find affordable, accessible, or high quality child care. It is a k 12 and workforce issue. That's the first place I'd spend a $100,000,000.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: Then I would restart the Knowles Nelson Stewardship Fund with another $100,000,000. Like, those are the types of things that we can do. That's bipartisan effort. Those are bipartisan things that have been successful. The Knowles Nelson Stewardship Fund, 90% of us live within a mile of a project that's been enhanced by that over the last forty years.

transcript.name: Joel Brennan
transcript.text: It's as bipartisan as it gets, and it now, as of July 1, doesn't exist anymore. Those are the types of things that we should be investing in.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Thank you. Mister Barnes, would you send it back to taxpayers or spend it? How would you spend it?

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: Well, let's first talk about how we got here. Now, the reason there is a surplus is because Republicans in the legislature have failed the people of Wisconsin. Our school districts are going to referendum every single year just to keep the lights on. And we also see gaps in health care because we are one of 10 states that has yet to extend our excuse me, expand our Medicaid program under the Affordable Care Act. We are in a world of trouble and Robin Vos has never been a good negotiating partner.

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: So no, I certainly wouldn't have signed the deal, but the way we give more money back to people, the way we actually return money to folks is by taxing the wealthy, taxing the billionaires, taxing these corporations that have been getting over on us, making money hand over fist while communities continue to starve for resources. This is how we can most effectively return money back to folks. On the issue of affordability, the best way we can close the affordability gap is to put more money in the pockets of hardworking people. Our minimum wage still $7.25 Costs have gone up, wages have not. But returning that money to the people, that means making the right investments in public education, making the investments in healthcare, taxing the wealthy, and implementing a working class tax cut for folks who work hard every single day and don't get the benefits that corporations get.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: So quickly, what are you doing with the surplus?

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: Well, with the surplus, like I said, it's just reinvesting back into education. And And also now also because of Trump's big ugly bill, there's gonna be some stresses when it comes to expanding BadgerCare, which I still support. It is the right thing to do for us. So many folks are staring down medical debt, medical bankruptcy. We're gonna

transcript.name: Matt Smith
transcript.text: move on to

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: taxes. We did bring up taxes, so let's move on to taxes. You all in some degree have used phrases like making the wealthy pay their fair share and discussed raising taxes on the rich to fund your priorities. Wisconsin already has the second highest top income tax rate in the Midwest at 7.65%, So so we want to know what all of you define as rich. So Mr.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Barnes, under your plan, what is the specific income level where taxes would go up and what percentage would that top tax bracket pay?

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: Yeah, so I think that incomes over $1,000,000 should be taxed a little bit higher, even if it's temporary. The fact is we are in a real crisis right now and our necessities have not been seeing the resources, have not been seeing the funding. Again, there's no reason these school districts should be going to referendum every single year just to fund basic services And if we increase that tax rate by less than 1%, 0.9%, 0.8%, we do a great deal to be able to provide much more funding to our school districts and also help close the share of revenues.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Is that what you're proposing? 0.8 or point 9%?

transcript.name: Mandela Barnes
transcript.text: Well, I'm saying this is all of I'm happy to negotiate. This is what we need to negotiate, but this is the arena where I'm in right now.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Miss Hong, the income level that you would raise taxes and how much?

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: Those who are making the million and $1. I think that, the billion as well to increase that 2.9%. It is incredibly disappointing that some of our lowest income earners are paying a higher tax rate than some of our highest income earners. We need to return to a progressive income tax rate. It is how we build sustainable revenue and ensure that we're able to actually increase our tax base across the state as more working class people are gonna be attracted to coming to Wisconsin to live, work, and play here.

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: I think that the legislation that I introduced, that would tax the billionaire and add a millionaire, tax bracket would lower property taxes by up to 44%, and we could put that funding into special education funding, which we have neglected to actually honor the budget amount, and we must bring that back up to 90% reimbursement.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: And the percentage for those millionaires?

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: I would increase that by about 1%.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: You would increase that to about, so about 8.65.

transcript.name: Francesca Hong
transcript.text: Correct.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Mr Crowley, your income level and and how much would you tax them?

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: Well, let's be very clear. It's just not the the income tax, but it's also the property taxes that are also extremely high in the state of Wisconsin.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: We'll talk about that next.

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: Okay, well, we talk about income taxes, what we really need to be focusing on is how do we actually fix this system moving forward? What we need to do is take a holistic view of our tax a our taxes here in the state of Wisconsin. The last time that we took a holistic view of how we spend our money and bring in revenues was in 1986 when governor Tommy Thompson was actually governor. And so we need to bring academics. We need to bring labor.

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: We need to bring business owners and community members to the table. And let's actually have a real discussion about the entire system. I don't think that we should be just focusing on how we can increase taxes just particular for for for certain income earners when we haven't looked at the entire system. When it comes down to those who are making hand over fist, we absolutely need to to tax the ultra wealthy. We need to be smart about how we're doing things long term.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Do you have an income level or a percentage for that?

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: Well, I think we always gotta look at those who are making more than a million dollars or more. Absolutely.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: And do you know how high you'd like to tax them?

transcript.name: David Crowley
transcript.text: No, I think that we have to look at the entire system holistically.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
transcript.text: Miss Roys, your income level and percentage you would tax them looking to raise taxes.

transcript.name: Kelda Roys
transcript.text: I agree with my colleagues that anyone who's earning over $1,000,000 a year should pay a slightly higher tax rate, but we also need to look at the corporate tax giveaways that have run rampant over the last fifteen years of Republican rule. We have rolled out the red carpet for Foxconn. The AI data center tax breaks are estimated to cost us $2,000,000,000. All that at a time when we are spending $0 on early childhood education, when our public schools have been starved of resources, jacking up people's property taxes just to help our kids keep teachers in the classroom. So as a small business owner, it offends me that the largest businesses in the state are not only not paying their fair share of taxes, but they're often getting public resources.

transcript.name: Kelda Roys
transcript.text: These are going to big polluters, big corporations, out of state corporations. They're not tied to job creation, and we need to not just tax the wealthy, but make sure that big corporations pay their fair share too.

transcript.name: Gerron Jordan
